n: *Study note:* *Psalm 111*. The psalmist praises God for his marvelous deeds, especially the way in which he provides for and delivers his people. The psalm is an acrostic. After the introductory call to praise, every poetic line (twenty-two in all) begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

*Translator's note:* For other uses of the Hebrew phrase וְהָדָרהוֹד (hod vehadar, “majesty and splendor”) see 1 Chr 16:27; {{Job 40:10|Job 40:10}}; {{Psalm 21:5|Pss 21:5}}; {{Psalm 96:6|96:6}}; {{Psalm 104:1|104:1}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “stands.”

*Translator's note:* Or “did,” if this refers primarily to the events of the exodus and conquest period (see vv. {{Psalm 111:6|6}}, {{Psalm 111:9|9}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a memorial he had made for his amazing deeds.”

*Translator's note:* Or “gave,” if the events of the exodus and conquest period (see v. {{Psalm 111:6|6}}, {{Psalm 111:9|9}}) are primarily in view.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who fear him.”

*Translator's note:* Or “he remembers his covenant forever” (see {{Psalm 105:8|Ps 105:8}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the strength of his deeds he proclaimed to his people, to give to them an inheritance of nations.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the deeds of his hands [are].”

*Translator's note:* That is, fair and for man’s good.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “done in faithfulness and uprightness.” The passive participle probably has the force of a gerund. See L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 89.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “redemption he sent for his people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he commanded forever his covenant.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the beginning of wisdom [is] the fear of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “good sense [is] to all who do them.” The third masculine plural pronominal suffix must refer back to the “precepts” mentioned in v. {{Psalm 111:7|7}}. In the translation the referent has been specified for clarity. The phrase שֵׂכֶל טוֹב (sekhel tov) also occurs in {{Proverbs 3:4|Prov 3:4}}; {{Proverbs 13:15|13:15}} and 2 Chr 30:22.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his praise stands forever.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 112*. This wisdom psalm lists some of the benefits of living a godly life. The psalm is an acrostic. After the introductory call to praise, every poetic line (twenty-two in all) begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Oh] the happiness [of] the man.” Hebrew wisdom literature often assumes and reflects the male-oriented perspective of ancient Israelite society. The individual is representative of a larger group, called the “godly” in vv. {{Psalm 112:3|3-4}}. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender specific “man” with the more neutral “one.” The generic masculine pronoun is used in the following verses.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fears.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in his commands he delights very much.” The words “in keeping” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Taking delight in the law is metonymic here for obeying God’s moral will. See {{Psalm 1:2|Ps 1:2}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “offspring”; *Heb* “seed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “His seed will be mighty on the earth, the generation of the godly.” The Hebrew term דוֹר (dor, “generation”) could be taken as parallel to “offspring” and translated “posterity,” but the singular more likely refers to the godly as a class. See BDB 189-90 s.v. for other examples where “generation” refers to a class of people.

*Translator's note:* In this context “light” symbolizes divine blessing in its various forms (see v. {{Psalm 112:2|2}}), including material prosperity and stability.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “merciful and compassionate and just.” The Hebrew text has three singular adjectives, which are probably substantival and in apposition to the “godly” (which is plural, however). By switching to the singular, the psalmist focuses on each individual member of the group known as the “godly.” Note how vv. {{Psalm 112:5|5-9}}, like vv. {{Psalm 112:1|1-2a}}, use the singular to describe the representative godly individual who typifies the whole group.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “man.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he sustains his matters with justice.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for an eternal memorial a just [one] will be.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his heart,” viewed here as the seat of the volition and emotions (see {{Psalm 108:1|Ps 108:1}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his heart,” viewed here as the seat of the volition.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he scatters, he gives.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stands forever.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his horn will be lifted up in honor.” The horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (see {{Deuteronomy 33:17|Deut 33:17}}; {{1 Kings 22:11|1 Kgs 22:11}}; {{Psalm 92:10|Ps 92:10}}). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt/lift up the horn” signifies military victory (see {{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Sam 2:10}}; {{Psalm 89:17|Pss 89:17}}, {{Psalm 89:24|24}}; {{Psalm 92:10|92:10}}; Lam 2:17).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the singular; the representative wicked individual is in view as typifying the group (note the use of the plural form in v. {{Psalm 112:10|10}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his teeth he will gnash.” In {{Psalm 35:16|Pss 35:16}} and {{Psalm 37:12|37:12}} this action is associated with a vicious attack.

*Translator's note:* This could mean that the desires of the wicked will go unfulfilled. Another possibility is that “desire” refers by metonymy to the object desired and acquired. In this case the point is that the wicked will lose what they desired so badly and acquired by evil means (see {{Psalm 10:3|Ps 10:3}}).
*Study note:* *Psalm 113*. The psalmist praises God as the sovereign king of the world who reaches down to help the needy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the rising of the sun to its setting.” The extent is not temporal (“from sunrise to sunset”) but spatial (“from the place where the sun rises [the east] to the place where it sets [the west].” In the phenomenological language of OT cosmology, the sun was described as rising in the east and setting in the west.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who makes high to sit.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who makes low to see.”
*Study note:* The language of v. {{Psalm 113:7|7}} is almost identical to that of {{1 Samuel 2:8|1 Sam 2:8}}.

*Study note:* *Psalm 114*. The psalmist recalls the events of the exodus and conquest and celebrates God’s kingship over his covenant people.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the house of Jacob from a nation speaking a foreign language.”

*Study note:* The psalmist recalls the crossing of the Red Sea ({{Exodus 14:21|Exod 14:21}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Jordan” (also in v. {{Psalm 114:5|5}}). The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* The psalmist recalls the crossing of the Jordan River ({{Joshua 3:13|Josh 3:13}}, {{Joshua 3:16|16}}).
*Study note:* *The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs*. This may recall the theophany at Sinai when the mountain shook before God’s presence ({{Exodus 19:18|Exod 19:18}}).

*Study note:* In v. {{Psalm 114:8|8}} the psalmist recalls the event(s) recorded in {{Exodus 17:6|Exod 17:6}} and/or {{Numbers 20:11|Num 20:11}} (see also {{Deuteronomy 8:15|Deut 8:15}} and {{Psalm 78:15|Ps 78:15-16}}, {{Psalm 78:20|20}}).

*Study note:* *Psalm 115*. The psalmist affirms that Israel’s God is superior to pagan idols and urges Israel to place their confidence in him.

*Translator's note:* Or “give glory.”

*Study note:* The psalmist asks the Lord to demonstrate his *loyal love and faithfulness*, not simply so Israel may benefit, but primarily so that the Lord will receive honor among the nations, who will recognize, contrary to their present view (see v. {{Psalm 115:2|2}}), that Israel’s God is committed to his people.
*Study note:* *He does whatever he pleases*. Such sovereignty is characteristic of kings (see Eccl 8:3).

*Translator's note:* The referent of the pronominal suffix is “the nations” (v. {{Psalm 115:2|2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the work of the hands of man.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they cannot mutter in their throats.” Verse {{Psalm 115:5|5a}} refers to speaking, v. {{Psalm 115:7|7c}} to inarticulate sounds made in the throat (see M. Dahood, *Psalms* [AB], 3:140-41).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will be.” Another option is to take the prefixed verbal form as a prayer, “may those who make them end up like them.”

*Study note:* Because the idols are lifeless, they cannot help their worshipers in times of crisis. Consequently the worshipers *end up* as dead as the gods in which they trust.

*Translator's note:* Or “[source of] help.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and their shield.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Translator's note:* Or “[source of] help.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and their shield.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[you] fearers of the Lord.” See {{Psalm 15:4|Ps 15:4}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “[source of] help.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and their shield.”

*Translator's note:* Or “remembers us.”

*Translator's note:* Another option is to translate the prefixed form of the verb “bless” in vv. {{Psalm 115:12|12-13}} as a jussive, “may he bless” (see v. {{Psalm 115:14|14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fearers of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the small along with the great.” The translation assumes that “small” and “great” here refer to age (see 2 Chr 15:13). Another option is to translate “both the insignificant and the prominent” (see {{Job 3:19|Job 3:19}}; cf. NEB “high and low alike”).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may he add to you, to you and your sons.” The prefixed verbal form is jussive, indicating this is a prayer.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the heavens [are] heavens to the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the sons of man.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “silence,” a metonymy here for death (see {{Psalm 94:17|Ps 94:17}}).

*Study note:* *Psalm 116*. The psalmist thanks the Lord for delivering him from a life threatening crisis and promises to tell the entire covenant community what God has done for him.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I love because the Lord heard my voice, my pleas.” It is possible that “the Lord” originally appeared directly after “I love” and was later accidentally misplaced. The translation assumes the prefixed verbal form is a preterite. The psalmist recalls that God heard his cry for help (note the perfect in v. {{Psalm 116:2|2a}} and the narrative in vv. {{Psalm 116:3|3-4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because he turned his ear to me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and in my days I will cry out.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “surrounded me.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun מֵצַר (metsar, “straits; distress”) occurs only here, {{Psalm 118:5|Ps 118:5}} and Lam 1:3. If retained, it refers to Sheol as a place where one is confined or severely restricted (cf. BDB 865 s.v. מֵצַר, “*the straits* of Sheol”; NIV “the anguish of the grave”; NRSV “the pangs of Sheol”). However, *HALOT* 624 s.v. מֵצַר suggests an emendation to מְצָדֵי (metsade, “snares of”), a rare noun attested in {{Job 19:6|Job 19:6}} and Eccl 7:26. This proposal, which is reflected in the translation, produces better parallelism with “ropes” in the preceding line.

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes the prefixed verbal form is a preterite. The psalmist recalls the crisis from which the Lord delivered him.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “guards.” The active participle indicates this is a characteristic of the Lord.

*Translator's note:* Or “the [morally] naive,” that is, the one who is young and still in the process of learning right from wrong and distinguishing wisdom from folly. See {{Psalm 19:7|Ps 19:7}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I was low.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “return, my soul, to your place of rest.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew idiom גָּמַל עַל (gamal ʿal) means “to repay,” here in a positive sense (cf. {{Psalm 13:5|Ps 13:5}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* “Lord” is supplied here in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “walk before” (see {{Psalm 56:13|Ps 56:13}}). On the meaning of the Hebrew idiom, see the notes at {{2 Kings 20:3|2 Kgs 20:3}}/{{Isaiah 38:3|Isa 38:3}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lands, regions.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a cup of deliverance I will lift up.” Perhaps this alludes to a drink offering the psalmist will present as he thanks the Lord for his deliverance. See v. {{Psalm 116:17|17}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “precious in the eyes of the Lord [is] the death of his godly ones.” The point is not that God delights in or finds satisfaction in the death of his followers! The psalmist, who has been delivered from death, affirms that the life-threatening experiences of God’s followers get God’s attention, just as a precious or rare object would attract someone’s eye. See {{Psalm 72:14|Ps 72:14}} for a similar expression of this belief.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I am your servant, the son of your female servant.” The phrase “son of a female servant” (see also {{Psalm 86:16|Ps 86:16}}) is used of a son born to a secondary wife or concubine ({{Exodus 23:12|Exod 23:12}}). In some cases the child’s father is the master of the house (see {{Genesis 21:10|Gen 21:10}}, {{Genesis 21:13|13}}; {{Judges 9:18|Judg 9:18}}). It may used metaphorically and idiomatically to emphasize the psalmist’s humility before the Lord and his status as the Lord’s servant. Or it may be a reference to the psalmist’s own mother who also was a servant of the Lord.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you have loosed my bonds.” In this context the imagery refers to deliverance from death (see v. {{Psalm 116:3|3}}).

*Study note:* *Psalm 117*. The psalmist tells the nations to praise the Lord for his loyal love and faithfulness.

*Translator's note:* Or “peoples” (see {{Psalm 108:3|Ps 108:3}}).
*Translator's note:* For this sense of the Hebrew verb גָּבַר (gavar), see {{Psalm 103:11|Ps 103:11}} and L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 17, 19.

*Study note:* *Psalm 118*. The psalmist thanks God for his deliverance and urges others to join him in praise.

*Translator's note:* Or “is forever.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the distress.” The noun מֵצַר (metsar, “straits; distress”) occurs only here and in Lam 1:3. In {{Psalm 116:3|Ps 116:3}} מֵצַר should probably be emended to מְצָדֵי (metsade, “snares of”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord answered me in a wide open place.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for me.”

*Translator's note:* The rhetorical question assumes the answer, “Nothing!” The imperfect is used in a modal sense here, indicating capability or potential. See {{Psalm 56:11|Ps 56:11}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “among my helpers.” The preposition may indicate identity here, while the plural may be one of majesty or respect.

*Translator's note:* “Taking shelter” in the Lord is an idiom for seeking his protection. Seeking his protection presupposes and even demonstrates the subject’s loyalty to the Lord. In the psalms those who “take shelter” in the Lord are contrasted with the wicked and equated with those who love, fear, and serve the Lord ({{Psalm 5:11|Pss 5:11-12}}; {{Psalm 31:17|31:17-20}}; {{Psalm 34:21|34:21-22}}).

*Study note:* The reference to an attack by *the nations* suggests the psalmist may have been a military leader.

*Translator's note:* In this context the phrase “in the name of the Lord” means “by the Lord’s power.”

*Translator's note:* Traditionally the verb has been derived from מוּל (mul, “to circumcise”) and translated “[I] cut [them] off” (see BDB 557-58 s.v. II מוּל). However, it is likely that this is a homonym meaning “to fend off” (see *HALOT* 556 s.v. II מול) or “to push away.” In this context, where the psalmist is reporting his past experience, the prefixed verbal form is best understood as a preterite. The phrase also occurs in vv. {{Psalm 118:11|11}}, {{Psalm 118:12|12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “were extinguished.”

*Translator's note:* The point seems to be that the hostility of the nations (v. {{Psalm 118:10|10}}) is short-lived, like a fire that quickly devours thorns and then burns out. Some, attempting to create a better parallel with the preceding line, emend דֹּעֲכוּ (doʿakhu, “they were extinguished”) to בָּעֲרוּ (baʿaru, “they burned”). In that case the statement emphasizes their hostility.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “pushing, you pushed me.” The infinitive absolute emphasizes the following verbal idea. The psalmist appears to address the nations as if they were an individual enemy. Some find this problematic and emend the verb form (which is a Qal perfect second masculine singular with a first person singular suffix) to נִדְחֵיתִי (nidkheti), a Niphal perfect first common singular, “I was pushed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to fall,” i.e., “that [I] might fall.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my strength and protection [is] the Lord.” The Hebrew term זִמְרָת (zimrat) is traditionally understood as meaning “song” (“my strength and song [is] the Lord”) in which case one might translate, “for the Lord gives me strength and joy” (i.e., a reason to sing). However, many recent commentators have argued that the noun זִמְרָת is here a homonym, meaning “protection” or “strength.” See *HALOT* 274 s.v.; cf. NEB “The Lord is my refuge and defence”; NRSV “my strength and my might.”

*Translator's note:* Or “salvation.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the sound of a ringing shout and deliverance [is] in the tents of the godly.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “does valiantly.” The statement refers here to military success (see {{Numbers 24:18|Num 24:18}}; {{1 Samuel 14:48|1 Sam 14:48}}; {{Psalm 60:12|Pss 60:12}}; {{Psalm 108:13|108:13}}).
*Translator's note:* The infinitive absolute emphasizes the following verbal idea.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the gates of justice.” The gates of the Lord’s temple are referred to here, as v. {{Psalm 118:20|20}} makes clear. They are called “gates of justice” because they are the entrance to the just king’s palace. This has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* Or “rejected.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the head of the corner.”

*Study note:* The metaphor of the *stone…the builders discarded* describes the way in which God’s deliverance reversed the psalmist’s circumstances. When he was in distress, he was like a stone which was discarded by builders as useless, but now that he has been vindicated by God, all can see that he is of special importance to God, like the *cornerstone* of the building.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it is amazing in our eyes.” The use of the plural pronoun here and in vv. {{Psalm 118:24|24-27}} suggests that the psalmist may be speaking for the entire nation. However, it is more likely that vv. {{Psalm 118:22|22-27}} are the people’s response to the psalmist’s thanksgiving song (see especially v. {{Psalm 118:26|26}}). They rejoice with him because his deliverance on the battlefield (see vv. {{Psalm 118:10|10-12}}) had national repercussions.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this is the day the Lord has made.” Though sometimes applied in a general way, this statement in its context refers to the day of deliverance which the psalmist and people celebrate.

*Study note:* A petition for deliverance and *success* seems odd in a psalm thanking God for deliverance, but it is not unique (see {{Psalm 9:19|Ps 9:19-20}}). The people ask God to continue to intervene for them as he has for the psalmist.

*Study note:* The people refer here to the psalmist, who enters the Lord’s temple to thank him publicly (see vv. {{Psalm 118:19|19-21}}), as *the one who comes in the name of the* Lord.

*Translator's note:* The pronominal suffix is second masculine plural, but the final mem (ם) is probably dittographic (note the mem [מ] at the beginning of the following form) or enclitic, in which case the suffix may be taken as second masculine singular, referring to the psalmist.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the house of the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he has given us light.” This may be an elliptical expression, with “his face” being implied as the object (see {{Numbers 6:25|Num 6:25}}; {{Psalm 31:16|Pss 31:16}}; {{Psalm 67:1|67:1}}; {{Psalm 80:3|80:3}}, {{Psalm 80:7|7}}, {{Psalm 80:19|19}}). In this case, “his face has given us light” = “he has smiled on us,” or “he has shown us his favor.” Another option (the one reflected in the translation) is that “light” here symbolizes divine blessing in the form of deliverance. “Light” is often used as a metaphor for deliverance and the life/blessings it brings. See {{Psalm 37:6|Pss 37:6}}; {{Psalm 97:11|97:11}}; {{Psalm 112:4|112:4}}; {{Isaiah 49:6|Isa 49:6}}; {{Isaiah 51:4|51:4}}; {{Micah 7:8|Mic 7:8}}. Some prefer to repoint the preterite form וַיָּאֶר (vayyaʾer, “he made light”) as a jussive וְיָאֵר (veyaʾer; “may he make light [for us]”).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun חַג (khag) normally means “festival,” but here it apparently refers metonymically to an offering made at the festival. BDB 291 s.v. חַג 2 interprets the word in this way here, citing as comparable the use of later Hebrew חֲגִיגָה, which can refer to both a festival and a festival offering (see Jastrow 424 s.v. חֲגִיגָה).

*Translator's note:* The second half of v. {{Psalm 118:27|27}} has been translated and interpreted in a variety of ways. For a survey of major views, see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 122.
*Study note:* *You are my God*. The psalmist speaks again (see v. {{Psalm 118:21|21}}), responding to the words of the worshipers (vv. {{Psalm 118:22|22-27}}).

*Translator's note:* The psalmist celebrates God’s law and the guidance it provides his people. He expresses his desire to know God’s law thoroughly so that he might experience the blessings that come to those who obey it. This lengthy psalm exhibits an elaborate acrostic pattern. The psalm is divided into twenty-two sections (corresponding to the letters of the Hebrew alphabet), each of which is comprised of eight verses. Each of the verses in the first section (vv. {{Psalm 119:1|1-8}}) begins with the letter alef (א), the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. This pattern continues throughout the psalm as each new section highlights a successive letter of the alphabet. Each verse in section two (vv. {{Psalm 119:9|9-16}}) begins with the second letter of the alphabet, each verse in section three (vv. {{Psalm 119:17|17-24}}) with the third letter, etc. This rigid pattern creates a sense of order and completeness and may have facilitated memorization.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Oh] the happiness of those who are blameless of way.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “walk in.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you, you commanded your precepts, to keep, very much.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “if only my ways were established.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will give you thanks with an upright heart.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not abandon me to excess.” For other uses of the phrase עַד מְאֹד (ʿad meʾod, “to excess”), see {{Psalm 38:6|Ps 38:6}}, {{Psalm 38:8|8}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “young man.” Hebrew wisdom literature often assumes and reflects the male-oriented perspective of ancient Israelite society. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, the gender specific “young man” has been translated with the more neutral “young person.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “purify his path.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by keeping according to your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss as well as the LXX read the plural, “your words.”

*Translator's note:* Or “hide.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your word.” Some medieval Hebrew mss as well as the LXX read the plural, “your words.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the way of your rules.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “as upon,” meaning “as if” (see 2 Chr 32:19).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all wealth.” The phrase refers to all kinds of wealth and riches. See {{Proverbs 1:13|Prov 1:13}}; {{Proverbs 6:31|6:31}}; {{Proverbs 24:4|24:4}}; {{Ezekiel 27:12|Ezek 27:12}}, {{Ezekiel 27:18|18}}.

*Translator's note:* The cohortative verbal forms in this verse express the psalmist’s resolve.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “gaze [at].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “ways” (referring figuratively to God’s behavior here).

*Translator's note:* The imperfects in this verse emphasize the attitude the psalmist maintains toward God’s law. Another option is to translate with the future tense, “I will find delight…I will not forget.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss as well as the LXX read the plural here.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is probably a cohortative indicating purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

*Translator's note:* The cohortative with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the imperative that begins the verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your word.” Many medieval Hebrew mss as well as several ancient versions read the plural here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “uncover.” The verb form גַּל (gal) is an apocopated Piel imperative from גָּלָה (galah, see GKC 214 §75.*cc*).

*Translator's note:* The cohortative with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose/result after the preceding imperative.

*Study note:* *Heb* This metaphor probably derives from Lev 25:23, which uses the terms גֵּר (ger, “resident foreigner”) and תּוֹשָׁב; (toshav, “resident/temporary settler”). *Study note:* *Meshech* was located in central Anatolia (modern Turkey). *Kedar* was located in the desert to east-southeast of Israel. Because of the reference to Kedar, it is possible that {{Psalm 120:5|Ps 120:5}} refers to a different Meshech, perhaps one associated with the individual mentioned as a descendant of Aram in 1 Chr 1:17. (However, the LXX in 1 Chr 1:17 follows the parallel text in {{Genesis 10:23|Gen 10:23}}, which reads “Mash,” not Meshech.) It is, of course, impossible that the psalmist could have been living in both the far north and the east at the same time. For this reason one must assume that he is recalling his experience as a wanderer among the nations or that he is using the geographical terms metaphorically and sarcastically to suggest that the enemies who surround him are like the barbarians who live in these distant regions. For a discussion of the problem, see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* (WBC), 146.

*Translator's note:* The singular participial form probably has a representative function here. The psalmist envisions the typical hater of peace who represents the entire category of such individuals.
